A Unified Geometric Framework for Weighted Contrastive Learning

Contrastive learning (CL) aims to preserve relational structure between samples by learning representations that reflect a similarity graph. Yet, the geometry of the resulting embeddings remains poorly understood. Here we show that weighted InfoNCE objectives can be interpreted as Distance Geometry Problems, where the weighting scheme specifies the target geometry to be realized by the representation. This viewpoint yields exact characterizations of the optimal embeddings for several supervised and weakly supervised objectives. In supervised classification, both SupCon and Soft SupCon (a dense relaxation of it where pairs from distinct classes have small non-zero similarity) collapse samples within each class to a single prototype. However, while balanced SupCon recovers the classical regular simplex geometry, class imbalance breaks this symmetry: SupCon induces non-uniform inter-class similarities depending on class sizes, whereas Soft SupCon preserves a regular simplex geometry regardless of class imbalance. In continuous-label settings, our framework reveals a different failure mode: [MATH y] -Aware CL generally cannot attain its entropic optimum unless the labels lie on a hypersphere, exposing a mismatch between Euclidean label weights and spherical latent similarity. By contrast, geometrically consistent choices such as Euclidean–Euclidean weighting or [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR admit unique optimal embeddings. Our results show that the choice of weighting scheme determines whether contrastive learning is geometrically realizable, degenerate, or inconsistent, providing a principled framework for designing contrastive objectives.
1 Introduction

Contrastive Learning (CL) plays a pivotal role in current supervised and self-supervised deep representation learning models. It was popularized through several successful frameworks: SimCLR Chen et al. (2020) and MoCo for self-supervised learning of visual representations, SupCon Khosla et al. (2020) for supervised classification, and CLIP Radford et al. (2021) for vision-language representation learning. Later on, it was adapted to perform supervised regression Zha et al. (2023); Barbano et al. (2023), handling continuous targets and weakly supervised learning Dufumier et al. (2021); Schneider et al. (2023) when auxiliary information (or meta-data) is available during training as a means of constraining representations. Despite their empirical success, the geometry of the representations learned by contrastive objectives remains poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear what structure these objectives are implicitly trying to realize in the embedding space, and whether this structure can always be achieved.

From a geometric perspective, CL can be viewed as attempting to realize a set of pairwise relationships between samples in a low-dimensional space. These relationships are specified implicitly by the weighting scheme used in the loss, which encodes prior knowledge about which samples should be similar or dissimilar. This raises a fundamental question: does there exist a representation satisfying these constraints, and if so, is it unique?

In this work, we show that weighted contrastive learning can be interpreted as a Distance Geometry Problem Liberti et al. (2014) (DGP), where the weighting scheme defines a target pairwise geometry. Under this view, learning representations amounts to finding a geometric realization of this target structure. This perspective reveals three regimes: some objectives define realizable geometries with unique solutions, others lead to degenerate solutions, and some are geometrically inconsistent.

In supervised classification, we prove that both SupCon and a soft relaxation of it collapse samples within each class, but differ under class imbalance: SupCon induces class-size-dependent prototype configurations, whereas the soft variant preserves a regular simplex geometry independent of imbalance. In continuous-label settings, we show that [MATH y] -Aware CL Dufumier et al. (2021) is generally inconsistent, while geometrically consistent formulations such as [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR Sobal et al. (2024) admit realizable and unique optima.

Beyond theory, this perspective provides practical guidance for designing contrastive objectives by matching the geometry induced by the weights with that of the embedding space. We also introduce metrics to evaluate convergence to the predicted optima and validate our results experimentally.
In summary, we make the following contributions:
We show that weighted InfoNCE defines a target pairwise geometry and that minimizing the loss amounts to solving a DGP.

We prove that both SupCon and Soft SupCon (a smooth relaxation in which inter-class pairs are assigned a small but non-zero similarity) collapse each class to a prototype, but differ under imbalance: SupCon produces class-size-dependent prototype geometry, whereas Soft SupCon preserves regular simplex geometry.

We show that the label-space geometry and latent-space similarity must be matched for the optimum to be realizable (e.g. as in [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR). As a consequence, we prove that [MATH y] -Aware CL generally cannot attain its entropic lower bound because it combines Euclidean label distances with spherical latent similarity.

We provide a novel lower bound for the value of the loss and provide three new metrics, all geometric in nature, as a principled means to evaluate the convergence of models and the optimality of their representations.
2 Related Work

Theoretical aspects of CL have mainly been studied from three perspectives: information theory, probability and graph theory, and metric learning. Our approach is in essence a geometric one and mostly aligns with this last view of CL.

Mutual information perspective. Early modern contrastive objectives were motivated by the fact that they can be understood as tractable proxies for mutual information (MI) maximization. Contrastive Predictive Coding van den Oord et al. (2018) introduced the InfoNCE loss and showed how negative sampling yields a scalable lower bound on MI in sequential prediction settings. In parallel, Deep InfoMax proposed MI maximization between global and local feature statistics for unsupervised representation learning Hjelm et al. (2018), and related multi-view MI objectives were developed for self-supervised learning Bachman et al. (2019). Subsequent work clarified the behavior and limitations of variational MI bounds (including InfoNCE) through bias–variance tradeoffs Poole et al. (2019). However, MI does not fully explain representation quality or geometry: empirical evidence Tschannen et al. (2020) shows that downstream performance strongly depends on architectural and estimator-induced inductive biases, rather than on MI estimation alone.

Probabilistic and graph-based view. Another line of research models positives as samples sharing an unobserved semantic factor (latent class), yielding generalization guaranties for downstream classification from contrastive pretraining Arora et al. (2019). More recent analyses shift from strong assumptions on latent-class sampling to augmentation-driven positive pairs by introducing an augmentation graph whose spectral structure is related to contrastive objectives HaoChen et al. (2021); HaoChen and Ma (2022). Stronger results were obtained on downstream performances with this formulation by assuming semantic clustering of this augmentation graph. Meanwhile, an attempt to unify contrastive and non-contrastive approaches was proposed Balestriero and LeCun (2022) based on a “similarity graph”, a rough approximation of the augmentation graph. A complementary view is given in Wang and Isola (2020) which interprets contrastive learning as trading off an alignment term (pulling positives together) and a uniformity term (uniformly spreading representations out on a hypersphere), while also noting the inherent limitations to learning this trade-off with limited data.

Metric Learning. Before the MI and probabilistic/graph-based perspectives of CL, early works on dimensionality reduction Hadsell et al. (2006) proposed a more geometric formulation of CL with subsequent pairwise and triplet-based losses, which explicitly enforce geometric structure in embedding space. Modern self-supervised Chen et al. (2020); He et al. (2020) CL frameworks can be seen as scalable extensions of this metric learning view that implicitly shape the geometry of representations on the unit sphere. In the discrete supervised setting, SupCon Khosla et al. (2020) extends self-supervised objectives using class labels to define positive samples. A more explicit geometric characterization was provided by Graf et al. (2021), which analyzes the loss-minimizing configurations of SupCon and states that, under idealized conditions, class representations approach a regular simplex arrangement on the hypersphere. In the regression case, kernel-based variants Dufumier et al. (2021); Barbano et al. (2023) and rank-based variants Zha et al. (2023) of the InfoNCE objective have been derived, but as far as we are aware a geometrical characterization of their optima has not been given until now.

Overall, while contrastive learning has been studied extensively from MI and probabilistic/graph-based viewpoints, a precise characterization of the geometry of optimal representations (including existence, uniqueness and the resulting distance structure) remains as of yet unexplored.
3 Analysis of Weighted Contrastive Learning

3.3 Connection with the Distance Geometry Problem
We can now express the relationship between the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss and the Distance Geometry Problem (DGP) Liberti et al. (2014) as immediate corollaries of Theorem 3.3:

When latent similarity is given by [MATH s_{ij}=-\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2}] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(-d_{ij})] for a symmetric dissimilarity matrix [MATH D=(d_{ij})] , attaining the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] stated in Theorem 3.3 amounts to solving the DGP
[MATH \|z_{i}^{*}-z_{j}^{*}\|^{2}=d_{ij}+c\qquad\textrm{for }i\neq j,] (2)
for any constant [MATH c\in\mathbb{R}] .

When [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(-{d_{ij}})] for a symmetric dissimilarity matrix [MATH D=(d_{ij})] , attaining the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] amounts to solving the cosine problem
[MATH \cos(z_{i},z_{j})=-\tau d_{ij}+c^{\prime}\qquad\textrm{for }i\neq j,] (3)
for any constant [MATH c^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}] .

These corollaries show that minimizing [MATH w] -InfoNCE amounts to finding a low-dimensional embedding with prescribed similarity, up to an additive constant [MATH c] or [MATH c^{\prime}] . We will go on to show that a mild condition on [MATH n] and [MATH \rank(D)] suffice to entail that [MATH c=0] or [MATH c^{\prime}=1] .
3.4 Existence and uniqueness of the optimal embedding

Having established the link between DGP and weighted InfoNCE, we ask ourselves the question of existence and uniqueness of solutions to these two families of problems. The answers involve a classical notion from computational geometry Alfakih and others (2018).
(EDM) An [MATH n\times n] matrix [MATH D=(d_{ij})] is called an Euclidean Distance Matrix (EDM) if there exist points [MATH z_{1}^{*},\dots,z_{n}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}] such that

We call the points [MATH z_{1}^{*},\ldots,z^{*}_{n}] a [MATH q] -dimensional realization of [MATH D] . The embedding dimension is defined as the smallest dimension [MATH r] of a Euclidean realization, or equivalently as the dimension of the affine span of any given Euclidean realization. Distinct Euclidean realizations of an EDM in a given dimension are congruent, i.e. they differ by a Euclidean isometry. A minimal Euclidean realization (i.e. in [MATH \mathbb{R}^{r}] ) is called a set of generating points of [MATH D] . Finally, we say that [MATH D] is spherical if those generating points can be chosen such that [MATH \|z_{1}\|=\cdots=\|z_{n}\|=\rho] for some radius [MATH \rho>0] . The smallest such [MATH \rho] is called the radius of a spherical EDM.

Assume that the number of points [MATH n] is strictly greater than [MATH 2q+3] . Assume that [MATH s_{ij}=\exp(-\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2})] and [MATH W=(\exp(-d_{ij}))] for [MATH D=(d_{ij})] an [MATH n\times n] dissimilarity matrix with [MATH \rank(D)\leq q+2] . Then the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] is attained iff [MATH D] is EDM of embedding dimension [MATH r\leq q] , up to diagonal elements. In that case, the minimum [MATH Z^{*}] satisfies [MATH \|z^{*}_{i}-z^{*}_{j}\|=d_{ij}] for all [MATH i,j\in[1..n]] and is essentially unique (i.e. up to Euclidean isometry).

3.5 Supervised classification: Soft SupCon
We now show that the Soft SupCon weighting scheme arises as a direct application of Theorem 3.8.

Let [MATH y_{i}\in[1..C]] be one of [MATH C] discrete classes associated with each sample and define [MATH w_{ij}=1] if [MATH y_{i}=y_{j}] and [MATH w_{ij}=\varepsilon\in(0,1)] otherwise. Assume [MATH n>2q+4] and consider [MATH s_{ij}=\exp(\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau)] . If [MATH C\leq q] and [MATH \tau\leq(C-1)/(-C\log\varepsilon)] , then the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] is attained by some [MATH Z^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}] , which is unique up to linear Euclidean isometry of the normalized embeddings. At the optimum, one has [MATH \cos(z_{i},z_{j})=1] when [MATH y_{i}=y_{j}] , and [MATH \cos(z_{i},z_{j})=1+\tau\log\varepsilon] otherwise. In particular, all points from the same class collapse to a single representation, and the [MATH C] classes form a simplex with uniform inter-class similarity [MATH \beta=1+\tau\log\varepsilon] . The simplex is regular when [MATH \tau^{*}=(C-1)/(-C\log\varepsilon)] , corresponding to [MATH \beta^{*}=-1/(C-1)] .
3.6 Supervised multivariate regression

Next, we state three results corresponding to various weighting schemes that can be encountered when using continuously labeled data (see Appendix C.1 for the proofs). Let [MATH (X,Y)] be a labeled dataset with [MATH \ell] continuous labels [MATH Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times\ell}] . We assume throughout that [MATH n>2q+4] so that Theorem 3.7 and 3.8 can be applied. Our first result concerns the case where Euclidean distance is used as a dissimilarity function in both label space and representation space.

Assume [MATH \ell\leq q] . If [MATH w_{ij}=\exp({-\|y_{i}-y_{j}\|^{2}})] and [MATH s_{ij}=-\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2}] , the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss attains its entropic lower bound in [MATH Z^{*}=(\widetilde{y}_{i})_{i=1}^{n}] , where [MATH \widetilde{y}_{i}=(y_{i},0,\dots,0)\in\mathbb{R}^{q}] for [MATH i\in[1..n]] , which is essentially unique.
Our next result is a negative one and concerns the Euclidean–spherical [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss, i.e. the [MATH y] -Aware loss Dufumier et al. (2021).

Even if [MATH \ell\leq q] , the [MATH y] -Aware InfoNCE loss, which is the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss with [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(-\|y_{i}-y_{j}\|^{2})] , does not attain the entropic lower bound unless the [MATH y_{i}] happen to lie on a hypersphere in [MATH \mathbb{R}^{\ell}] .
On the other hand, the spherical–spherical case, as in the [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR loss Sobal et al. (2024), does attain the entropic lower bound and offers a spherical counterpart to Theorem 3.10.

If [MATH \ell<q] and [MATH \tau\leq\tau^{\prime}] , the [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR loss Sobal et al. (2024), which is the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss with [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(\cos(y_{i},y_{j})/\tau^{\prime})] attains the entropic lower bound in the points [MATH z_{i}^{*}=(y_{i}/\|y_{i}\|,\sqrt{\tau^{\prime}/\tau-1},0,\dots,0)] for [MATH i\in[1..n]] . Moreover, that minimum is essentially unique.

In practice Sobal et al. (2024), the dimension of text embeddings in [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR is [MATH \ell=768] for CLIP and the latent dimension [MATH q=2048] for ResNet50. It was also found that [MATH \tau^{\prime}\approx\tau] gives the best classification accuracy on ImageNet.

Practical implications. Theorem 3.11 and 3.12 suggest that the pair of similarity functions used to define [MATH (W,S)] should be chosen consistently to allow for a realizable optimum. The spherical–spherical or Euclidean-Euclidean weighting schemes are therefore preferable over the Euclidean–spherical scheme (as in [MATH y] -Aware).
3.7 Sparse weights and limiting properties

The assumption of positive weights, i.e. [MATH w_{ij}>0] in Theorem 3.3, may be relaxed to [MATH w_{ij}\geq 0] assuming that [MATH \sum_{ik}w_{ik}>0] so that [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] is well defined: we term this the sparse case. Although any sparse matrix [MATH W] can be understood as a limit of a sequence of positive matrices [MATH (W_{m})] , the optimum of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] need not be the limit of the optimum of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W_{m}}] because in general convergence is not uniform. Moreover, the configuration of points which attain the minimum may behave qualitatively different in the limit.

In Appendix D.1 we prove that in the sparse case, the entropic lower bound continues to hold and that it is sharp. We give a necessary and sufficient for it to be optimal (i.e. impossible to improve upon). We go on to show that it is optimal in the case of the so-called Euclidean SupCon (i.e. the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss with a hard SupCon weighting scheme and Euclidean similarities [MATH s_{ij}=-\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2}] ) but that quasi-optima can be produced in any number of qualitatively distinct configurations. This comes in stark contrast to the soft case where optima are essentially unique (Theorem 3.7).
3.8 SupCon

We now consider the case of SupCon proper (i.e. the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss with a hard SupCon weighting scheme and spherical similarities [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] ). Using a compactness argument, we see in Appendix D.2 that the entropic lower bound is sub-optimal. We go on to prove the following theorem:
Let [MATH C] denote the number of discrete classes and [MATH \ell_{c}] the size of the [MATH c] th class. Assume that [MATH C\leq q] .
The SupCon loss has a unique global minimum over the matrices of the form [MATH G/\tau] , with [MATH G] an [MATH n\times n] cosine matrix.
That minimum has collapsed representations and can be expressed in terms of class prototypes [MATH \mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{C}\in\mathbb{S}^{q-1}] which are unique up to linear Euclidean isometry.
If [MATH c\neq c^{\prime}] , the value of [MATH \cos(\mu_{c},\mu_{c^{\prime}})] depends only on [MATH (\ell_{c},\ell_{c^{\prime}})] .

In particular we see that SupCon suffers from representation collapse which generalizes both Nguyen et al. (2024) and Behnia and Thrampoulidis (2024) in that we make no assumptions on [MATH \tau>0] nor do we require an infinite number of samples.

In the case of balanced classes, we easily recover the result from Graf et al. (2021) that SupCon optima correspond to regular simplices (Appendix D.2, Theorem D.6). Moreover, Hard and Soft SupCon have similar optima: both collapse classes and yield uniform inter-class similarities. For Hard SupCon, [MATH \beta_{\mathrm{hard}}=-1/(C-1)] depends on [MATH C] ; for Soft SupCon, [MATH \beta_{\mathrm{soft}}=1+\tau\log\varepsilon] depends on [MATH (\tau,\varepsilon)] but not on [MATH C] . Choosing [MATH \tau^{*}=(C-1)/(-C\log\varepsilon)] yields a regular simplex.
This equivalence breaks under class imbalance: SupCon produces non-uniform inter-class similarities, grouping minority classes more closely, whereas Soft SupCon is agnostic to class imbalance.
3.9 Metrics

To empirically evaluate whether the similarity structure of the learned encodings [MATH Z=(z_{1};\ldots;z_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}] are close to the theoretical optimum [MATH Z^{*}=(z_{1}^{*};\ldots;z_{n}^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}] as predicted by any of our theoretical results, we introduce three metrics.

The [MATH w] -InfoNCE entropic loss gap is defined as the nonnegative quantity [MATH \Delta_{W}:=({\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}}/{\min_{S}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}})-1] , where [MATH \min_{S}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] is the entropic lower bound stated in Theorem 3.3.

Note that a small value of [MATH \Delta_{W}] is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the [MATH z_{i}] to be close to the optimum [MATH z_{i}^{*}] . This motivates the introduction of a second metric, related to Kruskal’s stress, which directly compares the pairwise similarities of the [MATH z_{i}] versus those of the [MATH z_{i}^{*}] .

Let [MATH s:\mathbb{R}^{q}\times\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R}] denote a similarity function in latent space, e.g. [MATH s(x,y)=-\|x-y\|^{2}] or [MATH s(x,y)=\cos(x,y)] . The coefficient of similarity between [MATH Z] and [MATH Z^{*}] is defined as the [MATH r^{2}] of [MATH s(z_{i},z_{j})] as a predictor of [MATH s(z_{i}^{*},z_{j}^{*})] :

[MATH \displaystyle r^{2}_{s\textrm{-sim}}(Z,Z^{*})] [MATH \displaystyle:=1-\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{ij}\left[(s(z_{i},z_{j})-s(z_{i}^{*},z_{j}^{*}))^{2}\right]}{\widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{ij}[s(z_{i}^{*},z_{j}^{*})]}]
where [MATH \widehat{\mu}_{ij}] and [MATH \widehat{\sigma}^{2}_{ij}] denote, respectively, sample mean and sample variance over the set of pairs [MATH (i,j)\in[1..n]^{2}] .

Note by standard results that if [MATH s] is the negative squared Euclidean distance then [MATH r^{2}_{s\textrm{-sim}}=1] iff [MATH Z] and [MATH Z^{\prime}] differ by a Euclidean isometry. The same result holds if [MATH s] is cosine similarity and [MATH Z] and [MATH Z^{*}] are taken on the unit hypersphere. Note that the computation of [MATH r^{2}_{s\textrm{-sim}}] is [MATH O(n^{2})] in time, and therefore impractical for large [MATH n] . This motivates the following definition, which measures similarity at an intrinsic level in sub-quadratic [MATH O(n\log n)] time.
Let [MATH (\Omega,b)] minimize [MATH \sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\Omega z_{i}+b-z_{i}^{*}\|^{2}] over [MATH \Omega\in O_{q}(\mathbb{R})] , [MATH b\in\mathbb{R}^{q}] . The Procrustes similarity is defined by
[MATH r^{2}_{\mathrm{Proc}}(Z,Z^{*})=1-\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{i}\left[\|\Omega z_{i}+b-z_{i}^{*}\|^{2}\right]}{\widehat{\sigma}_{i}^{2}[z_{i}^{*}]},]
i.e. the coefficient of determination after optimal rigid alignment. Note that [MATH r^{2}_{\mathrm{Proc}}(Z,Z^{*})=1] iff [MATH Z] and [MATH Z^{*}] differ by a Euclidean isometry.
4 Experiments

Armed with the metrics defined in § 3.9, we conduct a series of experiments to validate our theoretical claims and verify whether representations learned with [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss on practical datasets are in fact near their geometric optima. Implementation details are provided in Appendix G.
4.1 Weighted InfoNCE on MNIST: discrete, continuous and mixed regime

We train a ConvNet with the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss on MNIST LeCun et al. (1998) across three regimes: (i) discrete classification, (ii) continuous regression, and (iii) mixed discrete–continuous labels.

Discrete case. We first consider the discrete classification setting, using Soft SupCon weights (as in § 3.5) with the value [MATH \varepsilon=e^{-1}] between negative samples. The optimal geometry corresponds to a regular 9-simplex, realizable in [MATH \mathbb{R}^{q}] for [MATH q\geq 9] . As shown in Fig. 2, both [MATH r^{2}_{s\text{-sim}}] and [MATH r^{2}_{\mathrm{Proc}}] increase with [MATH q] up to a sharp transition at [MATH q=9] , where the learned representation becomes nearly isometric ( [MATH r^{2}_{\mathrm{Proc}}\approx 0.9] ).

Multivariate regression. We then consider a continuous regression task based on two morphological attributes (thickness and slant). 5 Discussion and Open Problems

This work advances the understanding of weighted contrastive learning in both weakly supervised and supervised settings by explicitly characterizing the global optimal representation using a rigorous geometric framework. We derived conditions on weighting schemes to guarantee the existence of optimal realizations and introduced three novel metrics for assessing them. We made several rigorous predictions which we went on to confirm in practical applications.

Limitations. The main limitation of this work is that we assumed an explicit dissimilarity matrix encoding prior knowledge about the problem through labels or meta-data. In the self-supervised case (e.g. SimCLR Chen et al. (2020)), [MATH D] is a rough approximation of an implicit dissimilarity matrix across samples. Characterizing this matrix is difficult and should use empirical evidence and realistic assumptions Saunshi et al. (2022) as the basis for theoretical results. We leave this as an avenue for future research.

Overall, we believe that our geometric framework offers a fresh perspective on CL and SSL algorithms and a complementary approach to the mainstream probabilistic and graph-based views. We hope that our theoretical analysis of CL will be used by practitioners to better refine their weighting schemes, as well as by theorists to deepen their understanding of CL and SSL.
